finding.title: Unsigned HS256 token accepted when key is null (signature check skipped)
finding.evidence: With `createVerifier({key:null, algorithms:['HS256'], cache:false})`, `createVerifier` lets `null` through option validation because `typeof null === 'object'` satisfies the keyType check (line 392), so no error is raised for missing key material and `allowedAlgorithms` stays `['HS256']`. In `verifyToken`, `hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key` evaluates to false for `null` (line 180); the guard at lines 182-186 only throws `FAST_JWT_MISSING_KEY` when `!hasKey && signature` is true, i.e. only if a signature is present. The attacker-controlled token `base64url({alg:'HS256',typ:'JWT'}) + '.' + base64url(payload) + '.'` makes `decoder` return `signature = ''` (empty slice after the last '.'), which is falsy, so neither branch throws. `validateAlgorithmAndSignature` then passes the algorithm check (`HS256` is allowed) and skips signature verification entirely because of `if (signature && !verifySignature(...))` (line 139). Result: fully attacker-forged claims are accepted. PoC run against the local source printed `ACCEPTED: {"admin":true,"sub":"attacker"}` for the unsigned token, while the control with a non-empty signature correctly failed closed with `FAST_JWT_MISSING_KEY`, confirming the bypass is specifically the omitted-signature case. Missing key material does not fail closed; the intended 'HS256 authenticated only' policy is not enforced.

review_queue.evidence: The missingKey guard does not fire for an empty signature, so a null key with a signing algorithm accepts it. Confirmed by round4-jwt-verification.json.

finding.title: Issuer claim accepts an array, letting one allowed value authorize an attacker-controlled issuer/key source
finding.evidence: Input: a JWT whose payload.iss is an array of strings (e.g. ["https://evil.test","https://valid-iss"]). Flow: createVerifier with allowedIss registers an iss validator at line 475 without an `array` flag, unlike aud at line 471. In verifyToken the payload claim is taken at line 210; lines 211-212 convert an array into `values`; line 221 calls validateClaimType, but that function (lines 144-152) only uses the `array` flag to choose the error-message wording and never rejects an array, so the array passes type checking. Line 226 then calls validateClaimValues(values, claim, allowed, arrayValue), whose check at line 159 is `values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v)))`; because `.some` over the array elements succeeds if ANY element equals the configured allowedIss, the whole token is accepted. Protection failure: there is no enforcement that iss is a single string, and validateClaimValues applies any-element-matches semantics appropriate for aud to the scalar iss claim. PoC executed against this exact source (createVerifier requiring ./src/verifier.js with real HS256): single unexpected iss 'https://evil.test' => REJECTED FAST_JWT_INVALID_CLAIM_VALUE, while iss ['https://evil.test','https://valid-iss'] => ACCEPTED. Exploitability in the stated threat model: the keyFetcher uses jwt.payload.iss as the JWKS domain, and the PoC key fetcher logged domain=https://evil.test for that accepted array (first element), so the signature is verified with the attacker's key fetched from the attacker's domain while the decoy allowed value passes line 159. This is not a universal bypass on its own: it requires the async key function that derives the key source from the same iss claim (as in get-jwks providerDiscovery); with a fixed key the array still makes an otherwise-rejected issuer pass, but the authentication impact comes from the key fetch trusting payload.iss.

review_queue.evidence: Payload validator loop for the issuer/claim array; same expected issuer-array root cause.

finding.title: Cached verification bypasses exp for tokens lacking iat, allowing expired-token replay
finding.evidence: Cache entries built in cacheSet only derive a token-specific expiry bound when payload.iat is a number (hasIat guard, line 89): inside that block exp is clamped at lines 96-97. When a signed HS256 token carries exp but no iat (iat is optional per RFC 7519), the guard is false, so cacheValue[2] (max) stays 0; line 106 then sets it to maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL (default cacheTTL from line 384 is 600000 ms / 10 min). The success payload is cached with that bound. On a subsequent replay the cache-hit branch in verify (lines 257-272) returns the cached payload whenever min===0 and now<=max, without re-running the exp validator, so the token stays accepted for up to cacheTTL after exp. Demonstrated locally: an HS256 token {sub:'alice',exp:now+2} with no iat, verified once with cache:true, is replayed 3s later (past exp). A cache:false verifier on the same token rejects with FAST_JWT_EXPIRED (control), but the cache:true verifier returns the payload (ACCEPTED). A control token that also includes iat is correctly rejected (FAST_JWT_EXPIRED) under cache:true, confirming iat absence is the discriminator. An attacker who captured any valid token therefore gets an expiry-enforcement bypass/authorization replay window of up to cacheTTL (10 min by default), needing no signing key.

review_queue.evidence: cacheSet derives the cached validity window only when a numeric iat exists, so cache:true keeps accepting a signed exp token without iat after expiry. round4-jwt-verification.json shows uncached and numeric-iat controls reject; cache opt-in is required.

finding.title: Lock acquisition truncates attacker-chosen file via symlink in lock path (O_TRUNC without O_NOFOLLOW)
finding.evidence: In the Unix lock-acquisition path, `UnixFileLock._acquire` builds `open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` and then calls `os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode)` (sink, line 44). The flags lack both `os.O_NOFOLLOW` and `os.O_CREAT|os.O_EXCL`, so `os.open` resolves the final path component itself and follows a symlink there; `O_TRUNC` then truncates whatever file the link targets to zero bytes. The path is the lock file inside a directory the threat model says an unprivileged local attacker can write. The attacker replaces the lock path with a symlink (e.g. `lockdir/mylock.lock -> ../secrets/secret.txt`, a sibling secrets file the service later writes). On the next `FileLock(...).acquire()`, line 40's `ensure_directory_exists` leaves the link in place, line 42's `Path(self.lock_file).exists()` follows the link so no `O_CREAT` is added, and line 44 opens and truncates the victim secrets file rather than locking the intended lock file. The `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` at line 46 and `fcntl.flock(fd, ...)` at line 48 then act on the victim file descriptor. Neither `_util.raise_on_not_writable_file` nor any pre-open `os.path.islink`/`lstat` check is performed on the lock path, and there is no atomic `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` guard, so caller/attacker-controlled `lock_file` reaches the truncating `os.open` unvalidated. Because the directory is attacker-writable, the symlink is stable across the check/open sequence, making the truncation reachable without a race. The same `O_TRUNC` also truncates the lock file on every acquisition even without a symlink, but the security-relevant path is the attacker-planted symlink redirecting truncation onto a file the attacker does not own. PoC source at pocsym_test.py was written to place `lockdir/mylock.lock -> ../secrets/secret.txt`, seed the secret with `TOP SECRET DATA`, acquire the lock, and assert the secret is emptied; execution could not be completed here because the sandbox's `python3` shim exits rc=49 without running (the package under audit is at /tmp/.tmpd6UueP), so the impact is established from the inspected source semantics and the platform's standard symlink-following `open(2)` behavior rather than from a completed run.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Cache expiry derived from exp ignores maxAge, allowing token replay past maxAge
finding.evidence: Configured with key=HS256 secret, cache:true, maxAge:1000ms. On first successful verify, cacheSet computes the cache validity window. At lines 95-100 the exp branch takes precedence: when payload.exp is a number, cacheValue[2] = payload.exp*1000 + clockTolerance, and the maxAge branch (else-if at line 98, using iat*1000+maxAge) is never reached. For a normally issued token iat < exp, exp is later than iat+maxAge, so the cached max is bounded only by exp (or the 600s default cacheTTL at line 105), not by the 1000ms maxAge. The cache-hit path (lines 257-272) then returns the stored payload directly at line 271 via handleCachedResult without re-running verifyToken, so the iat/maxAge date validator (lines 462-464) is skipped entirely. PoC run of the actual src: token iat=N, exp=N+100s, maxAge=1000ms; first verify within maxAge returns 'attacker'; after ~1500ms a cache:false verifier rejects with 'The token has expired' (maxAge enforced), but the cache:true verifier still returns 'attacker' — the maxAge lifetime limit is bypassed on cache hits, letting a holder replay the token until exp/cacheTTL. Required configuration: cache enabled and maxAge set shorter than the token exp, which is exactly the intended use of maxAge.

review_queue.evidence: cacheSet maxAge branch; same cached-lifetime root cause with an alternate CWE.

finding.title: ChunkedReader discards chunk terminator without validating it is CRLF, enabling chunk-body framing disagreement
finding.evidence:
Attacker controls the chunked body. In this h11 (0.14.0) source, after a chunk's data bytes are consumed, ChunkedReader sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2 (line 197) and on the next call blindly skips those two bytes: data = buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard) (line 164), self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data) (line 167). The two discarded bytes are never checked to equal b"
"; the ABNF chunk_header regex (h11/_abnf.py lines 125-131) validates only the size line, and validate() in _util.py is never applied to the terminator. Any two bytes are accepted as the chunk footer, including a bare LF (b"A
") followed by the first byte of the next chunk-size line, or b"XX". I reproduced this locally: feeding SERVER h11 the body b"1
A
15
HELLO
0

" (data chunk "A", LF-only terminator, then "15" = 0x15) produced h11 events Data(b'A'), Data(b'HELLO'), EndOfMessage — h11 consumed LF as the terminator and reinterpreted the following bytes as the next chunk header. Cross-parser difference: a strict RFC 7230 parser requires CRLF after chunk data and rejects that byte sequence (a strict reference parser raised before any HELLO chunk), while a bare-LF-tolerant parser instead consumes the LF terminator and reads the same remainder as a chunk of length 0x15, yielding a different chunk boundary for the same byte stream. Because the sink (line 164) also stops mid-unit when only one of the two footer bytes is buffered (line 168-169), the same desync exists for split reads. This is the framing disagreement that is the documented precondition for HTTP request smuggling when h11 sits in a chain with a second, differently strict chunked parser; it is a parser-confusion/de-sync condition rather than a completed exploit by itself. The upstream h11 0.16.0 reader was changed to store the expected footer as b"
" and raise LocalProtocolError on mismatch (this baseline 0.14.0 lacks that check), confirming the missing validation is the root cause.

review_queue.evidence: The _bytes_to_discard branch consumes the unvalidated chunk footer; same framing root cause as the expected line-197 sink.

finding.title: chacha20() passes an unvalidated key pointer to crypto_chacha20_djb, which reads 32 bytes unchecked
finding.evidence: The Python-facing wrapper chacha20(key, nonce, message) (c_monocypher.pyx:257) validates only the nonce length (line 266/268) and never checks len(key). When nonce is the valid 8 bytes required by the audit scope, control reaches line 269: crypto_chacha20_djb(result, message, len(message), key, nonce, 0). Cython compiles the `const uint8_t key[32]` parameter as a bare pointer: the generated C (c_monocypher_gen.c:5447) does `__pyx_t_12 = __Pyx_PyObject_AsUString(__pyx_v_key)` (macro -> __Pyx_PyObject_AsString, i.e. PyBytes_AS_STRING) and passes that raw pointer with no length check. The native sink crypto_chacha20_djb (monocypher.c:225) unconditionally executes `load32_le_buf(input + 4, key, 8);`, reading 8 consecutive little-endian u32 words = the full 32 key bytes regardless of the actual size of the caller's key buffer. Therefore a caller passing a key shorter than 32 bytes (e.g. b'' or b'\x00') triggers an out-of-bounds read of up to 31 bytes past the end of the buffer into adjacent heap/allocator memory, which is undefined behavior and can fault when the buffer abuts an unmapped page. The protection present elsewhere in the module (cdef class IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption checks `len(key) != 32` at c_monocypher.pyx:214; lock/unlock and other primitives document 32-byte keys) is absent from chacha20(), so the length contract is not enforced before the pointer reaches the native read.

review_queue.evidence: The 24-byte nonce branch of chacha20 also omits the key-length check. Same chacha20 wrapper bounds root cause as line 267.

finding.title: Unvalidated argon2 nb_blocks under-allocates work area in argon2i_32
finding.evidence: The public API argon2i_32(nb_blocks, ...) (c_monocypher.pyx:322) takes a caller-controlled nb_blocks and writes it directly into config.nb_blocks (line 328) without the _validate_u32 check applied to other length fields and without enforcing Monocypher's documented minimum (monocypher.h:160 requires nb_blocks >= 8 * nb_lanes). The work area is then allocated at the sink line 345 as malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024) and handed to crypto_argon2 at line 347. Inside the C routine the effective block count is derived by integer division: segment_size = config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4; lane_size = segment_size * 4; nb_blocks = lane_size * config.nb_lanes (monocypher.c:752-754), rounding nb_blocks DOWN to a multiple of 4*nb_lanes. With the wrapper fixing nb_lanes=1 (line 330), nb_blocks in {0,1,2,3} yields segment_size=0 and lane_size=0, i.e. an effective block count of 0. However, the initialization loop unconditionally writes two full 1024-byte blocks per lane, blocks[l*lane_size + i] for i in {0,1} (monocypher.c:776-783), so it stores 2048 bytes starting at the base of the work area regardless of the effective count. For nb_blocks=1 the wrapper allocates only 1024 bytes but the C routine writes 2048 bytes (1024-byte heap overflow); for nb_blocks=0 malloc(0) is called and 2048 bytes are written past a zero-size allocation (or past NULL when malloc returns NULL). The same lane_size=0 makes last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1 = blocks - 1 and store64_le_buf(final_block, last_block->a, 128) read 1024 bytes before the work area (monocypher.c:902,911), an out-of-bounds read. Additionally, because the multiplication in line 345 is performed in size_t, on 32-bit targets nb_blocks values whose product exceeds 2^32 wrap to a tiny allocation while the C routine still uses the full rounded block count, producing an arbitrarily large overflow. The wrapper performs no range/minimum validation on nb_blocks, so a caller or attacker-supplied work factor of 0 or 1 drives an out-of-bounds write.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: chacha20() does not validate key length, causing out-of-bounds key read
finding.evidence: chacha20() validates the nonce length (24 or 8, lines 266-272) but never checks the key length. crypto_chacha20_x (line 267) and crypto_chacha20_djb (line 269) are declared with `const uint8_t key[32]`; Cython passes the caller's bytes pointer directly and the C code unconditionally loads 32 key bytes (monocypher.c:219-235 crypto_chacha20_djb does load32_le_buf(input+4, key, 8) = 32 bytes; crypto_chacha20_x reads key via crypto_chacha20_h). A key shorter than 32 bytes produces a heap out-of-bounds read of up to 31 bytes beyond the supplied buffer, exposing adjacent process memory through the generated keystream/XOR output and risking a fault. No length guard exists anywhere on the key path.

review_queue.evidence: chacha20 validates the nonce length but not the key length; the native operation reads 32 key bytes. Genuine wrapper bounds defect, matches its own promoted case.

finding.title: key_exchange()/compute_key_exchange_public_key() accept short keys causing out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: key_exchange(your_secret_key, their_public_key) (line 375) and compute_key_exchange_public_key(secret_key) (line 362) forward caller bytes into crypto_x25519 / crypto_x25519_public_key without any length validation. The C prototypes declare fixed 32-byte buffers and unconditionally read 32 bytes from each input (monocypher.c:1557 crypto_x25519_public_key -> crypto_x25519, which reads secret_key[0..31] and their_public_key[0..31]); Cython performs no size check when converting the Python bytes to the pointer. Passing a secret or public key shorter than 32 bytes yields a heap out-of-bounds read of up to 31 bytes, letting attacker-influenced input drive an X25519 computation over adjacent memory (confidentiality loss/oracle) and potentially crashing.

review_queue.evidence: key_exchange reads fixed-size native buffers without a wrapper length check; same wrapper bounds family.

finding.title: signature_check() accepts short signature/public_key causing out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: signature_check(signature, public_key, message) passes both buffers directly to crypto_eddsa_check (line 429) with no length checks, while only the message length is supplied explicitly. The C declaration expects `signature[64]` and `public_key[32]`, and crypto_eddsa_check reads all 64 signature bytes and all 32 public-key bytes; Cython converts the Python bytes to a raw pointer without validating size. A caller supplying a signature shorter than 64 bytes or a public key shorter than 32 bytes triggers a heap out-of-bounds read of up to 63/31 bytes past the buffer, allowing adjacent memory to be consumed as signature/key material and potentially causing a crash. Compare signature_sign/compute_signing_public_key, which do validate secret-key length (lines 392-393, 412-413), showing the omission is specific to the verification path.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: IntoIter drop double-drops elements when an element destructor panics
finding.evidence: In `<IntoIter<T> as Drop>::drop` (line 2541), `drop_non_singleton` moves the backing `ThinVec` out into local `vec` (line 2546), then destroys the still-unconsumed tail with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547). The length/cleanup state is only committed afterward by `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If an element's `Drop::drop` panics, slice `drop_in_place` runs its guard, destroys the remaining tail elements, and then unwinds at line 2547 before line 2548 executes. During unwinding the local `vec` (a `ThinVec<T>`) is itself dropped: `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917) calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the full `[0, len)` range because the length was never updated. This re-drops: (a) elements `[start, len)` that were already destroyed (double free / double drop), and (b) already-yielded elements `[0, start)` whose values were moved out by `next` (line 2510) (drop of a moved-out value / use-after-move). Demonstrated with a safe-code PoC (type with a panicking `Drop`) built against this crate: output shows `drop Elem(2)` panicking, then cleanup `drop Elem(3)`, `drop Elem(4)`, then re-drops `drop Elem(1)`, `drop Elem(2)`, `drop Elem(3)`, `drop Elem(4)` and abort with 'panic in a destructor during cleanup'. Protections failed because the decrement/zeroing of the vector length occurs only after the unwinding sink, so no guard updates the length before element destruction runs.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result dereferenced in argon2i_32 (NULL-pointer availability failure)
finding.evidence: A Python caller controls nb_blocks; it is stored unvalidated into the 32-bit config.nb_blocks at line 328, so any value 0..0xFFFFFFFF is accepted. Line 345 does `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024))` and never inspects the return value. A large nb_blocks (e.g. 4_000_000 => ~4 GiB, or 0xFFFFFFFF => ~4 TiB) makes malloc fail and return NULL, which is passed directly to crypto_argon2 at line 347. That function uses work_area as its block array (stores to blocks[...] at monocypher.c:781 and the wipe ZERO(p, 128*nb_blocks) at monocypher.c:915), so it writes through the NULL pointer and segfaults the interpreter. The try/finally only frees the pointer; there is no NULL check or MemoryError path, so the failed large allocation is an unhandled availability failure rather than a Python exception.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 consumes the malloc result without a NULL check; distinct allocation-failure path from undersized work area.

finding.title: Unvalidated small nb_blocks yields a too-small Argon2 work area and heap out-of-bounds access
finding.evidence: Monocypher requires config.nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes and a work area of nb_blocks*1024 bytes (monocypher.h:160). argon2i_32 performs no lower-bound validation: it sets nb_lanes=1 and config.nb_blocks=nb_blocks (lines 328-330), then allocates exactly nb_blocks*1024 bytes at line 345. For nb_blocks<4, crypto_argon2 derives segment_size = nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4 = 0 and lane_size = 0 (monocypher.c:752-754), yet the initial fill loop unconditionally writes two blocks per lane, blocks[0] and blocks[1] (monocypher.c:776-781). With nb_blocks=1 the allocation is only 1024 bytes, so writing blocks[1] is a 1024-byte heap out-of-bounds write; nb_blocks=0 makes malloc(0) even smaller. Independently, lane_size=0 makes last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1 = blocks - 1 (monocypher.c:902) and store64_le_buf(final_block, last_block->a, 128) reads 1024 bytes before the buffer (monocypher.c:911), folding adjacent heap bytes into the hash returned to the caller. Thus this is a successful-but-too-small allocation leading to heap corruption/over-read, distinct from the NULL-pointer failure above.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Double-drop in IntoIter::drop when an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: The Drop impl for IntoIter<T> (src/lib.rs:2539) forwards to `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544), which at line 2547 executes `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` and then unconditionally calls `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 2548. This function is unsound for any partial view of the vector: if an element's Drop panics while unwinding the half-open slice `[start..]`, the `set_len_non_singleton(0)` at line 2548 is skipped, so the moved-out-of iterator's backing ThinVec still claims a nonzero length pointing at already-dropped slots. When that ThinVec is subsequently dropped (or cleared), the same slots are dropped again, and `start` also remains stale. Attack surface is ordinary safe code: `let mut v = ThinVec::new(); v.push(elem0); v.push(elem1); let mut it = v.into_iter(); it.next(); drop(it);` with an element type whose Drop unwinds. Local PoC run against this crate source confirms the defect: after catching the panic, counters read `into_iter: panicked=true first_is_some=true` and `INTO_ITER drops per element (sound=[0,1,1]) = [1, 2, 2]` — element 1 (the one whose Drop panicked) is dropped twice. The correct 0.2.16+ code introduces a DropGuard that calls set_len_non_singleton(0) during unwinding; the audited 0.2.15 implementation has no such guard, making this a double-free reachable without unsafe from the public API.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Issuer claim accepts an array of strings, letting an attacker pair an allowed `iss` with one used for key lookup
finding.evidence: Input: `createVerifier({ key: keyFetcher, allowedIss: 'https://valid-iss' })` where `keyFetcher` (e.g. get-jwks providerDiscovery) derives the JWKS domain from `jwt.payload.iss`. Flow: the `iss` validator is registered at line 475 WITHOUT the `array` flag used for `aud` (line 471). In verifyToken the array-ness is only checked by element type and is never rejected: line 211 `arrayValue = Array.isArray(value)` and line 221 `validateClaimType(values, claim, array, ...)` iterates the elements, so any array of strings passes type validation regardless of the (unused) `array` flag. The value check then reaches the sink at line 159 `if (!values.some(v => allowed.some(a => a.test(v))))`: because it uses `values.some(...)`, validation succeeds if ANY single element equals the allowed issuer, so extra attacker-chosen elements are ignored by the check. Failed protection: there is no enforcement that `iss` (declared `iss?: string` in src/index.d.ts:108) is a scalar; the `array` option has no functional effect and `validateClaimValues` never requires all elements to match. Configuration/impact: with the dynamic key fetcher, an attacker submits `iss: ['https://attacker.example','https://valid-iss']`; line 159 accepts it because one element matches `allowedIss`, and the same `payload.iss` is passed to `getAsyncKey`/`keyFetcher` (src/verifier.js:319), which resolves keys using that claim, so the attacker-paired issuer drives the key source and a token signed by the attacker-controlled key is accepted. PoC (run against src/verifier.js in the audit root) confirms: a plain unexpected string `iss` is rejected, but `iss: ['https://attacker.example','https://valid-iss']` signed with an attacker key is ACCEPTED, with `keyFetcher` observing the attacker-controlled `payload.iss`. This is not a standalone bypass: it requires a key fetcher that trusts `payload.iss` as the key domain.

review_queue.evidence: The issuer-array expected sink with an alternate CWE.

finding.title: Symlink-following O_TRUNC open lets attacker truncate arbitrary sibling file via lock path
finding.evidence: In UnixFileLock._acquire (filelock/_unix.py:39-44) the lock path is opened with `open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC` (line 41) via `os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode)` (line 44, the sink). os.open() follows symbolic links and no O_NOFOLLOW is set; the pre-check `Path(self.lock_file).exists()` (line 42) also follows links and does no lstat/inode verification, and fchmod/flock only occur after the file has already been truncated. Because the attacker is stated to have write access to the directory containing the lock path, they can unlink the lock file and replace it with a symlink pointing at a sibling file (e.g. the secrets file the service writes). When the service acquires the lock, os.open() resolves the symlink to the attacker-chosen target and O_TRUNC zeroes it, so the attacker selects which file is truncated. Demonstrated locally: replicating the exact flag computation of lines 41-44 and opening a directory entry that links to a sibling 'secrets.txt' left that file at size 0 with empty contents (`os.open(link, O_RDWR|O_TRUNC, 0o644)` -> 'TRUNCATED'); the local run used a hardlink fallback only because this host forbids unprivileged symlink creation, and on Unix a writable directory permits symlinks directly, with identical O_TRUNC-follows-link kernel semantics. No validation (O_NOFOLLOW, lstat+S_ISLNK rejection, or fstat inode comparison) prevents the substitution.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Cached-token expiry not enforced for tokens without iat (exp ignored, accepted for cacheTTL past expiration)
finding.evidence: Configuration in scope: HS256 verified with a real secret key and cache:true (default cacheTTL=600000ms, clockTolerance=0); tokens carry `exp` but may omit `iat`. Flow: verify() looks up the LRU cache (lines 257-272) and, on a miss, validates the signature/claims and stores the success payload via cacheSet (line 312 / 357). Inside cacheSet, the token time-window bounds are computed ONLY when `hasIat` is true (line 89 guards lines 92-102): `cacheValue[2]` is set from `payload.exp * 1000 + clockTolerance` at line 97. When the token has `exp` but no numeric `iat`, `hasIat` is false, so lines 92-102 are skipped and `cacheValue[2]` remains 0. Line 106 then overwrites it with `maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL`, i.e. first-verification time + 600000ms, completely ignoring `payload.exp`. The cache read condition (lines 266-268, `max === 0 || now <= max`) therefore returns the stored success for up to cacheTTL after the first successful verification, even after `exp` has passed. The exp validator at lines 452-459 is never consulted again on a cache hit. PoC (poc_expiry_bypass.js, executed): sign `{sub:'victim', exp: now+2}` (no iat) with HMAC-SHA256/real secret, verify with cache:true -> accepted and cache entry `max - now = 600000ms`; after sleeping 2.5s past exp, the uncached verifier rejects with FAST_JWT_EXPIRED while the cached verifier still returns the payload ('EXPIRY BYPASSED'). Root cause: the `hasIat` gate makes exp/nbf-based cache bounds conditional on an optional claim, so expiry is silently replaced by cacheTTL; a replayed expired token (or a token whose remaining lifetime is shorter than cacheTTL) is accepted, defeating session expiration/authorization.

review_queue.evidence: cacheValue fallback to cacheTTL; same cached-lifetime root cause.

finding.title: Unconstrained selector index bypasses ItemAtIndex comparator, yielding an all-zero SHA256 output
finding.evidence: In the standalone Sha256General template the compression-output selector index is derived from prover-controlled data and fed into a bit-width-sensitive comparator without a matching width constraint. paddedInLength is a bare signal input (line 97; set from the also-bare input at Sha256Bytes line 19/33) and is only tied down by `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111). The only length check is `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength; ... out === 1;` (lines 125-128), which does not range-check paddedInLength and, crucially, imposes no lower bound on inBlockIndex. Line 195 then feeds `inBlockIndex - 1` into `arraySelectors[k].index` of `ItemAtIndex(maxBlocks)` (line 191); that value is never constrained to `log2Ceil(maxBlocks)` bits. ItemAtIndex performs `lessThan = LessThan(bitLength); lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1;` (array.circom lines 25-28), and circomlib's LessThan is only sound when its inputs are < 2^bitLength — a precondition violated here. Concrete forging witness: set paddedInLength = 0, so inBlockIndex = 0 and index = 0 - 1 = p-1 (the BN254 scalar field prime). LessEqThan(0, maxBitLength) = 1, so the length check passes; LessThan evaluates (p-1 + 2^bitLength - maxBlocks) mod p = 2^bitLength - maxBlocks - 1, which is a small non-negative value below 2^bitLength, so `lessThan.out === 1` is satisfied even though p-1 >> maxBlocks. No IsEqual(i, p-1) matches for i in [0, maxBlocks), so CalculateTotal's sum is 0 and `out[k] <== arraySelectors[k].out` (line 196) is 0 for all 256 bits — the prover obtains an all-zero hash for arbitrary input. A Python model of the exact circomlib LessThan/LessEqThan/Num2Bits field arithmetic (model_check.py) reproduces this for maxByteLength 64/128/512/1024: L=0 gives LessEq(out)=1, index=p-1, ItemAtIndex LessThan.out=1, eq_match=False. This is limited to the standalone template/witness soundness; no claim is made that the full EmailVerifier's end-to-end scheme is broken, since its additional constraints prevent this witness.

review_queue.evidence: Sha256General/Sha256Partial derive inBlockIndex from an unbounded paddedInLength and feed inBlockIndex-1 into ItemAtIndex, whose LessThan lacks a range check. Same comparator/selector soundness defect as the expected line-126 sink.

finding.title: Cache TTL ignores maxAge, allowing replay of tokens past their maxAge lifetime
finding.evidence: With cache:true and maxAge:1000, a signed HS256 token carrying numeric iat and a later exp is validated once, then stored by cacheSet(). In cacheSet (lines 89-106) the expiry bound cacheValue[2] is derived ONLY from payload.exp when present: line 96-97 sets cacheValue[2] = payload.exp*1000 + clockTolerance, and the maxAge branch at line 98 (payload.iat*1000 + maxAge) is reached only when exp is absent. The computed bound is never reduced to iat+maxAge, so the stored entry stays a cache hit until min(exp, now+cacheTTL) (default cacheTTL 600000ms, lines 105-106). The cache-hit path in verify() (lines 257-272) then returns the previously validated payload without re-running the maxAge validator added at lines 462-464, so the iat/exp validity check that the non-cached path enforces is bypassed. The issue and coverage of the flaw in blocking replays within the maxAge window are demonstrated by the local PoC on the audited source: with cache:false, a token replayed after maxAge (3s > 1s/3s window) is rejected with 'The token has expired'; with cache:true the identical replay is accepted ('first=OK | replay after maxAge=OK (accepted)'). Required configuration: cache enabled (true/numeric size) plus a numeric maxAge and a token whose exp is later than iat+maxAge; attacker prerequisite is possession of a legitimately issued token, which they replay after maxAge but before exp and within cacheTTL.

review_queue.evidence: cacheSet exp branch; same cached-lifetime root cause as the maxAge case.

finding.title: Undersized Argon2 work-area allocation leads to heap out-of-bounds write for caller-controlled nb_blocks
finding.evidence: Python callers control nb_blocks, which is copied straight into config.nb_blocks at c_monocypher.pyx:328 with no minimum/multiple validation, and the work area is sized from the same value at the allocation sink c_monocypher.pyx:345: `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * (<size_t> 1024))`. The C routine then derives its own effective geometry at monocypher.c:752-754 (`segment_size = config.nb_blocks / config.nb_lanes / 4; lane_size = segment_size * 4; nb_blocks = lane_size * config.nb_lanes`), i.e. it rounds nb_blocks DOWN to a multiple of 4*nb_lanes. However, before any of those sizes are used, monocypher.c:776-783 unconditionally fills the first 2 blocks of every lane: `FOR_T(u32,l,0,config.nb_lanes){ FOR_T(u32,i,0,2){ ... load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size + i].a, hash_area, 128); } }`. This loop does not depend on segment_size/lane_size, so it always writes exactly 2 blocks (2*1024 = 2048 bytes) per lane even when the rounding yields lane_size == 0. Because the wrapper never enforces the header's documented requirement `nb_blocks >= 8 * nb_lanes` (monocypher.h:160) nor a multiple of 4*nb_lanes, a caller passing nb_blocks = 1 (nb_lanes is fixed to 1) makes segment_size = 1/1/4 = 0 and lane_size = 0, yet malloc only reserves 1*1024 = 1024 bytes while the C code writes blocks[0] and blocks[1] = 2048 bytes, a 1024-byte heap buffer overflow (nb_blocks = 0 gives malloc(0) and a 2048-byte overflow). A local arithmetic model of the exact C expressions confirms allocation 1024 vs written 2048 for nb_blocks=1 and 0 vs 2048 for nb_blocks=0, while nb_blocks>=2 no longer overflows. The same lane_size==0 condition also makes monocypher.c:902 `last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1` point one block before the allocation. Neither runtime nor compile-time validation protects this (the only checks, _validate_u32, are applied to password/salt/key/ad lengths, not to nb_blocks, and malloc's NULL result is not checked).

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: Chunked reader blindly discards two footer bytes instead of validating CRLF, producing cross-parser framing ambiguity
finding.evidence:
Input: an attacker-controlled chunked body reaches ChunkedReader.__call__ after a complete chunk is consumed; line 196-197 sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2 (a bare integer count, line 154), and the next invocation takes the branch at line 163, calling buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard) at line 164 and decrementing the counter at line 167 solely by length (self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)). The extracted bytes are never compared against b"
"; _receivebuffer.maybe_extract_at_most (h11/_receivebuffer.py:77-85) just slices any bytes, and the code then asserts only the count is zero (line 171). Consequently any two octets after the chunk data — e.g. body b"5
AAAAA0

" (CR CR terminator) or b"5
AAAAA

0

" (LF LF) — are silently swallowed and the reader proceeds to the next chunk header/terminal 0 chunk, whereas an RFC 7230-conformant chunked parser requires chunk-data to be followed by exactly CRLF and rejects those bytes as a chunk-footer violation. A second contributing leniency is in the header grammar (h11/_abnf.py:124-131): chunk_ext = ";.*" permits arbitrary text including CR/LF-bearing extensions, and trailing OWS before the chunk_header CRLF is accepted, so h11's notion of where chunk data ends can differ from a stricter reverse-proxy chunked parser. Required configuration: h11 used as the body parser on one side of a proxy chain where the front end and h11 disagree on footer/extent bytes (the precondition for request smuggling). This is a demonstrated cross-parser disagreement, not a completed exploit: the body bytes after the terminator are re-parsed by the peer as a new message only if the front end forwards them, which depends on the specific front-end's boundary handling. The fix in h11 0.16.0 changes _bytes_to_discard to the byte string b"
" and raises LocalProtocolError on footer mismatch, confirming the audited 0.14.0 code lacks this validation.

review_queue.evidence: The _bytes_to_discard branch consumes the unvalidated chunk footer; same framing root cause as the expected line-197 sink.

finding.title: chacha20() 8-byte-nonce path passes an unvalidated, undersized key buffer to C crypto_chacha20_djb (out-of-bounds read)
finding.evidence: chacha20(key, nonce, message) (c_monocypher.pyx:257) validates only the nonce length (24 vs 8, lines 266-272); there is no check that len(key) == 32 anywhere in the wrapper (a search for 'len(key)' / '!= 32' in c_monocypher.pyx returns no matches). When the caller supplies an 8-byte nonce, control reaches line 269: crypto_chacha20_djb(result, message, len(message), key, nonce, 0). Cython converts the Python bytes/bytearray key object to a const uint8_t* pointing at its backing buffer (only len(key) bytes are allocated), but the native signature declares key[32] (c_monocypher.pyx:127) and the implementation unconditionally reads a full 32-byte key: monocypher.c:219-226 does load32_le_buf(input, chacha20_constant, 4) then load32_le_buf(input+4, key, 8), i.e. 8 little-endian 32-bit words = 32 bytes read from key. If the Python caller passes a key shorter than 32 bytes (e.g. chacha20(b'shortkey', nonce8, msg)), the C code reads up to 28 bytes past the end of the key buffer. Protections are absent: the C function has no length parameter for the key and cannot bound it, and the wrapper never rejects short keys. A negative/short key therefore causes a heap out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory whose bytes are folded into the ChaCha20 key, producing an incorrect/observable keystream and, for keys near the end of an allocation or for non-bytes buffers, a process crash (availability). The same uncontrolled-key pattern exists throughout the wrapper (e.g. lock/unlock, blake2b), but the reachable sink under the stated scope is line 269. No compiled monkey testing was possible in this environment (no C compiler was available to build the extension), so this finding rests on inspected source: the unvalidated Python key buffer flows directly to a fixed 32-byte native read.

review_queue.evidence: The 24-byte nonce branch of chacha20 also omits the key-length check. Same chacha20 wrapper bounds root cause as line 267.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops backing vector elements when an element's Drop unwinds
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` -> `drop_non_singleton` moves the `ThinVec` out of the iterator with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` into local `vec` (line 2546), then destroys only the unconsumed suffix with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) and only afterwards resets the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). The length is a single length prefix (indices 0..start were already `ptr::read` out by `Iterator::next`, line 2510, but the header len still counts them). If an element's `Drop` panics, unwinding skips line 2548, so the local `vec` is dropped by its own `ThinVec::drop` (line 1917: `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) over the *full* `[0..len]` range. This re-drops (a) elements already moved out by `next()` (a use-after-move) and (b) the very elements just destroyed by the failing `drop_in_place`, producing double-drop/double-free. Contrast `ThinVec::truncate` (lines 1061-1063), which decrements the length *before* `drop_in_place` to be panic-safe; the IntoIter path lacks any such guard. Reachability: `ThinVec<T>` with a panicking `Drop` impl on `T`, obtained via `into_iter()`, only partially consumed, then dropped. Local PoC (rustc 1.90, gnu target) with `Elem(i)` panicking on drop of id 1 and `thin_vec![Elem(0),Elem(1),Elem(2)]`, consuming one element then `drop(it)` under `catch_unwind`, printed `Elem0=2 Elem1=2 Elem2=2` (expected 1 each), confirming double-drop of all three elements.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc for argon2 work_area causes NULL-pointer dereference (DoS)
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 lets a Python caller set nb_blocks with no upper bound. At line 345, work_area = malloc((size_t)nb_blocks * 1024); the return value is never checked for NULL before line 347 calls crypto_argon2(hash, 32, work_area, ...). For a large but valid value (e.g. nb_blocks = 0xFFFFFFF0), Cython's __Pyx_PyLong_As_size_t succeeds and the multi-terabyte request causes malloc to return NULL. crypto_argon2 immediately treats work_area as a blk* (monocypher.c:757) and writes blocks[0]/blocks[1] (monocypher.c:781), dereferencing NULL and crashing the process. No NULL guard or allocation-size limit exists, so a caller-controlled nb_blocks reliably triggers a denial-of-service crash. This is distinct from an under-sized buffer: here the allocation fails entirely and the pointer is NULL.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 consumes the malloc result without a NULL check; distinct allocation-failure path from undersized work area.

finding.title: Unvalidated nb_blocks yields under-sized work_area and heap out-of-bounds write
finding.evidence: nb_blocks is passed to malloc at line 345 and to config.nb_blocks at line 328 without the _validate_u32 guard used for password/salt/key/ad and without enforcing the documented minimum nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes (monocypher.h:160). When nb_blocks is 0 or 1, malloc succeeds with a 0- or 1024-byte buffer, but crypto_argon2 always writes 2 blocks (2048 bytes) per lane: segment_size = nb_blocks/1/4 = 0 so lane_size = 0, and the initialization loop load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size + i].a, ...) for i in 0..1 (monocypher.c:776-782) writes blocks[0] and blocks[1], i.e. 2048 bytes, into a buffer smaller than 2048 bytes. This is a successful-but-too-small allocation leading to an out-of-bounds heap write, unlike the NULL-pointer case where the allocation fails outright. It is triggerable on 64-bit platforms (no integer overflow needed) purely by supplying nb_blocks < 2.

review_queue.evidence: Unvalidated nb_blocks sizes the work area while native Argon2 reads initialized blocks; same expected undersized-work-area root cause with an alternate CWE at the expected line.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops elements when an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: `impl Drop for IntoIter` at src/lib.rs:2539-2556 moves the inner vector into a local `vec` (line 2546) and then calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) before zeroing the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any element's `Drop` panics (safe code), unwinding skips line 2548, so the local `vec` is dropped with its original length during unwind; `Drop for ThinVec::drop_non_singleton` again calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) over the same already-destroyed elements, double-freeing them. Trigger is safe-only: obtain a `ThinVec` of panicking-drop elements, call `.into_iter()`, and drop the iterator; default `std` build. PoC `tests/poc_drop_panic.rs::into_iter_panicking_drop_double_drops` observed `total_drops=6` for 3 live elements (2x per element), while the `truncate` control showed no double drop.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.
